query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of boron to phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys will improve their glass-forming ability and enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
generation.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy that exhibits marginal glass-forming ability and moderate thermal stability of its amorphous phase.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled minor addition (on the order of 1–5 atomic percent) of boron during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: The intervention is expected to be effective when the alloy is processed by rapid quenching to bypass crystallization. Its benefit is anticipated in cases where the alloy exhibits significant mixing enthalpy and atomic size mismatch. The effect may be diminished if boron is added in excessive amounts or if the cooling rate is insufficient.
generation.structural_mediator: The boron atoms are expected to increase local chemical heterogeneity and improve atomic packing efficiency by enhancing negative mixing enthalpy, thereby deepening the free-energy well of the amorphous state.
generation.mechanism: Boron, when added in minor amounts, is likely to bond strongly with phosphorus and other constituent elements. This interaction can impede the short-range atomic ordering that precedes crystallization. By increasing the atomic size mismatches and enhancing negative heats of mixing, the new atomic configurations hinder nucleation events that would otherwise lead to crystallization, thus improving both the glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy without boron, the boron-containing alloy will require a higher critical cooling rate to avoid crystallization and will demonstrate an increased crystallization onset temperature (or delayed exothermic peaks in DSC measurements), indicating enhanced thermal stability of the amorphous structure.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy without any boron addition, processed under similar rapid quench conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected within a narrow boron concentration window (approximately 1–5 at.%). The intervention may not yield the predicted effect if the boron content is too high (which could lead to other phase formations) or if the quenching and processing conditions are not sufficiently rapid to promote amorphous formation.
generation.uncertainty: While analogous mechanisms of minor alloying additions improving phase stability are documented in high-entropy alloys, the specific influence of boron in phosphorus-containing systems remains uncertain. The optimal boron concentration and processing conditions require further empirical determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples having identical base phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy compositions: one set with a controlled addition of approximately 3 at.% boron and one set without boron. Rapidly quench both sets to obtain an amorphous structure. Subject the samples to controlled heating while recording thermal events using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and perform structural analysis (e.g., XRD, TEM) to monitor crystallization.
measurements: DSC to record crystallization onset temperatures and exothermic peaks
Critical cooling rate measurements to assess glass-forming ability
XRD and TEM for phase identification and quantification of amorphous versus crystalline structures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in crystallization onset temperature or do not require a higher critical cooling rate to stay amorphous (when compared to the undoped baseline), then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. As a result, precipitation strengthening should be considered in developing HEAs for high temperature applications.
